profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for an internal proposal to extend the company's code review bot so it can automatically identify personal data processing in pull requests for the checkout platform. The proposal combines static code analysis with metadata from existing schemas to generate review comments and a lightweight processing summary for reviewers. The agenda is to decide whether the current design is sufficient for a pilot in the checkout area, what parts of the system the pilot is assumed to cover, and whether the output is adequate for both engineering review and privacy analysis. The expected outcome is conditional approval of the design for a pilot, with both participants believing they agree on scope, evidence quality, and how the bot will identify personal data handling.

members.name: Asha Raman
members.expertise: Static analysis, CI/CD systems, code review automation, developer tooling
members.background: Asha leads the internal review-bot platform used across backend teams and previously built low-latency linting and code ownership checks for Java and Kotlin services.
members.private_state: She wants approval for a lightweight pilot this quarter that can run inside existing PR latency budgets and avoids requiring application teams to maintain new annotations or inventories.
hidden_assumptions: In a code review context, 'personal data processing' mainly means explicit reads, writes, transformations, or transmissions visible in the application code being changed.
A pilot in 'checkout' naturally means the checkout-api repository and the code paths directly modified in new pull requests, not adjacent infra or shared contract repos.
The 'existing catalog' to reuse is the developer-facing schema metadata already attached to OpenAPI fields and ORM models.
A design is 'ready for pilot' if it can post low-noise comments on new PRs and catch the main personal-data touchpoints, even if broader inventory accuracy is incomplete.
Review output should stay brief and repository-local; anything beyond that can be filled in manually after the bot flags likely issues.

members.name: Martin Keller
members.expertise: Privacy-by-design, GDPR implementation, data inventories, architecture review
members.background: Martin previously led security architecture reviews and now owns engineering guidance for data mapping, retention controls, and privacy review processes across product teams.
members.private_state: He wants this design to become a durable source of evidence for privacy analyses so the company stops maintaining separate, incomplete data-mapping documents by hand.
hidden_assumptions: In privacy terms, 'personal data processing' includes framework-driven logging, tracing, event publication, temporary buffering, and downstream storage even when developers do not write that code explicitly.
A pilot in 'checkout' reasonably includes the service repo plus deployment manifests, event contracts, and nearby shared definitions that determine where data goes.
The 'existing catalog' to reuse is the central privacy data inventory and glossary already maintained for records-of-processing work.
A design is 'ready for pilot' only if its output can be used repeatedly as evidence for DPIA or record updates without major manual reconstruction.
Slightly richer review output is acceptable if it improves traceability across teams and systems.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the bot should identify 'personal data processing' in code review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Asha means explicit handling visible in changed application code, such as reading a customer email, copying it into a DTO, or writing it to a database call.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Martin means the full set of privacy-relevant operations, including logs, traces, event emission, framework-managed persistence, and other indirect handling triggered by the code path.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term sounds shared and authoritative, and both participants are cooperative professionals who assume the phrase already has an obvious meaning in this context, so neither pauses to unpack the legal-versus-tooling interpretation.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'checkout' pilot scope
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss running the pilot 'for checkout' or 'in the checkout service.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Asha assumes scope is the checkout-api repository and the files changed in PRs there, possibly including repository-local config files.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Martin assumes scope includes the broader checkout processing boundary: repo code, deployment manifests, emitted event schemas, and other nearby artifacts that define downstream data movement.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Cross-functional teams routinely refer to a product area by one shorthand name, and the design review focuses on approval rather than enumerating boundaries, so each person silently fills in the scope from their own work habits.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'existing catalog' the design will reuse
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the proposal should 'reuse the existing catalog' for personal-data labels.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Asha is thinking of the developer portal's API/schema metadata, where fields like customer_email and billing_address already carry internal tags used by documentation tooling.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Martin is thinking of the privacy office's central data inventory and glossary used for records of processing and DPIA templates.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are genuinely existing catalogs of data-related labels inside the company, and each participant rarely interacts with the other's one, so the phrase feels specific enough without prompting clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about whether the proposal is 'ready for a pilot next sprint.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Asha believes readiness means the bot can run on new checkout PRs with acceptable latency, produce concise comments, and be good enough for engineers to manually follow up on edge cases.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Martin believes readiness means the pilot output is stable and structured enough to serve as reusable evidence for privacy analysis, not just an engineering hint that requires significant reconstruction later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Design reviews often end with a simple ready/not-ready judgment, and both members assume the underlying standard is obvious from prior pilot discussions, even though one is optimizing for rollout practicality and the other for auditability.

turns.inner_thought: This should be the last design check before I get the green light for a lightweight pilot next sprint. I need Martin comfortable without turning this into a giant privacy inventory project. For me, 'personal data processing' here is the obvious code-review version: explicit handling in the PR diff, like reading customer fields, moving them through DTOs, and writing them out. And 'for checkout' means the checkout-api repo on new PRs. If we can stay inside current PR latency budgets and post concise comments, it's ready.
